waitListSize.description: The number of messages waiting due to flow control configuration.

parallelismMax.description: The configured maximum number of messages allowed to run concurrently, if parallelism is set.

parallelismCount.description: The current number of messages running in parallel.

rateMax.description: The configured maximum number of messages allowed per rate period, if rate limiting is set.

rateCount.description: The number of messages dispatched in the current rate period.

ratePeriod.description: The length of the rate period in seconds.

ratePeriodStart.description: Unix timestamp (seconds) when the current rate period started.

isPinnedParallelism.description: True if the flow-control key has a pinned parallelism configuration.

isPinnedRate.description: True if the flow-control key has a pinned rate configuration.

isPaused.description: True if the delivery of messages associated with the flow-control key is paused.

patches.why: The two documents give GET /v2/flowControl and GET /v2/flowControl/{flowControlKey} one FlowControlKey schema each, and they differ: qstash's has eleven fields with `waitListSize`, workflow's two with `waitlistSize`. One server answers both documents' clients, so one of them is wrong. The vendor's own client decodes qstash's: @upstash/qstash 2.11.3 (the version Dub's @upstash/workflow resolves) types the answer as FlowControlInfo with `flowControlKey`, `waitListSize` (capital L), `parallelismMax`, `parallelismCount`, `rateMax`, `rateCount`, `ratePeriod`, `ratePeriodStart`, `isPaused`, `isPinnedParallelism` and `isPinnedRate`. So workflow's schema is replaced with qstash's, byte for byte.

source.quote: type FlowControlInfo = { /** * The flow control key. */ flowControlKey: string; /** * The number of messages waiting in the wait list. */ waitListSize: number;

patches.why: Both documents give POST /v2/messages/{messageId}/retry (one endpoint on one server: a step waiting for its retry is a QStash message), and they differ only in workflow's listing a 500 Internal Server Error. A server fault is not a behaviour of the operation a twin decides, and the qstash document's answer set for the same endpoint is 200, 400 and 404; the 500 is removed from workflow's so the union holds qstash's answers.

source.quote: 200 description The message is rescheduled for immediate delivery. 400 description The message id is invalid, or the message belongs to a queue.

value.name: cancel
value.description: true cancels the run; false reports it finished, its route function having returned (the body is the run's result).

patches.why: The vendor's own client ends every run through this operation with a `cancel` query parameter the document does not list: @upstash/workflow 1.3.0 (the version Dub installs) reports a run whose route function returned with `DELETE /v2/workflows/runs/<id>?cancel=false` and the run's result as the body (`triggerWorkflowDelete`), and a cancel from inside the run with `?cancel=true` (`makeCancelRequest`).

value.name: source
value.description: workflow lists the failed workflow runs (Upstash Workflow's DLQ) instead of QStash's failed messages.

patches.why: @upstash/workflow 1.3.0's `client.dlq.list` reads the Workflow DLQ at QStash's own `GET /v2/dlq` with `source=workflow` in the query, not at the `GET /v2/workflows/dlq` the workflow document names.

source.quote: path: ["v2", "dlq"], method: "GET", query: { cursor, count, ...filter, source: "workflow" }

patches.why: With `source=workflow` the list is the Workflow DLQ, whose entries the client types as the workflow document's DLQ message (a failed run: `dlqId`, `workflowRunId`, `workflowUrl`, ...), so the answer is either envelope: QStash's failed messages, or the failed workflow runs.

source.quote: path: ["v2", "dlq"], method: "GET", query: { cursor, count, ...filter, source: "workflow" }

value.description: The unique id within the DLQ

patches.why: The DLQ's retry and delete name a message by its `dlqId` (their `dlqIds` parameter), and the vendor's client types every DLQ message as carrying one; the document's DLQMessage leaves it out.

source.quote: type DlqMessage = Message & { /** * The unique id within the DLQ */ dlqId: string;

post.description: A workflow run waits at a `context.waitForEvent` step for the event id: the waiter holds the run's URL, the step and its timeout, until a notify for the event resumes the run or the timeout does.

parameters.name: eventId
parameters.description: The event id the run waits for.

timeout.description: a duration: a number and s, m, h or d

step.description: the wait step: stepId, stepType, stepName, concurrent, targetStep

200.description: The run waits for the event.

patches.why: @upstash/workflow 1.3.0's `context.waitForEvent` step is submitted to `POST /v2/wait/<eventId>` (`LazyWaitEventStep.submitStep`), with the run's URL, the timeout, the URL and headers to call when it times out, and the step (`getBody`), and the run id in its headers; neither document has the path. The client does not read the answer (`parseResponseAsJson: false`); where the evidence stops, the answer is a 200 with no body.

The vendor's own clients pause a schedule with PATCH, not the POST the document names: @upstash/qstash 2.11.3's `schedules.pause` sends `method: "PATCH"` to /v2/schedules/<id>/pause, as qstash-py 3.4.0's `schedule.pause` does. So the server answers PATCH there as it answers POST; the operation is the document's POST, copied.

The vendor's own clients resume a schedule with PATCH, not the POST the document names: @upstash/qstash 2.11.3's `schedules.resume` sends `method: "PATCH"` to /v2/schedules/<id>/resume, as qstash-py 3.4.0's `schedule.resume` does. So the server answers PATCH there as it answers POST; the operation is the document's POST, copied.
